list.listitem: Concussion includes a spectrum of manifestations that can range from transient mild symptoms to ongoing disabling problems. C
Players with previous concussion are more likely to have recurrent concussion. B
Women and athletes with three or more prior concussions are more likely to sustain more severe concussions. B
Athletes should have physical and cognitive rest for 24-48 hours after a concussion, followed by resuming sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise. B
Approach the return to activity in a systematic, stepwise fashion as tolerated based on symptoms. Prescribed bed rest is not required.C

background.definition: Concussion is a clinical syndrome characterized by immediate and transient alteration in brain function after direct and/or indirect forces to the head causing neurometabolic dysfunction.

list.listitem: 0.81 per 1000 athlete exposures. ("Athlete exposure" is one athlete participating in one practice or game.)
In athletes <18 years of age, there is an estimated 1.1 to 1.9 million sports- and recreation-related concussions annually, with more than half occurring during non-organized activities.
In college athletes, the overall rate of concussion was 4.2 per 1000 athlete exposures.
In high school, the overall rate of concussion was 17 per 100,000 athlete exposures.
Annual cost of acute care and rehabilitation in the United States for new cases of traumatic brain injury (TBI) is estimated at $9 to $10 billion.
Estimates for average lifetime cost of care for a person with severe TBI range from $600,000 to $1,875,000.
Blunt force trauma.
Sudden acceleration, deceleration, and rotational forces.
No existing animal or experimental model accurately represents concussion.
Concussion is the result of rapid movement of the brain within the skull that imparts shearing or torsional forces to neural tissue followed by metabolic and mechanical changes.

The neurometabolic cascade that details the complex processes that result from concussion injury was previously identified. Following injury, there is a significant ionic flux within neurons, along with glutamate release which increases the brain's energy demands, thus causing a metabolic crisis until processes can be restored.
This complex cascade has been shown to render neural tissue more susceptible to further injury, with an increased risk for recurrent concussion and the development of postconcussion syndrome.
If neuropsychological testing is used in the diagnosis, treatment, or return to play for athletes following concussion, then baseline testing is recommended. C
Preseason neuropsychological baseline testing of all athletes is the recommended model for use of concussion screening instruments in sports, if available.
Comparison with an athlete’s preinjury performance on a given measure provides the most accurate indicator of postinjury recovery.

High risk concussion features include: female athletes, participating in soccer and basketball; body checking in ice hockey, a body mass index >27 and training for <3 hours per week; playing American football; and Australian rugby.
There is no clinical trial evidence that currently available protective equipment will prevent concussion.
Rule changes to reduce head injury rate may be appropriate when a clear-cut mechanism is implicated in a particular sport.
The use of correctly fitting mouth-guards may reduce cerebral injury.
Neck muscle conditioning may be of value in reducing impact forces on the brain.

The most important aspect is the education of players, coaches, and physicians regarding the detection of concussion, its clinical features, assessment techniques, and principles of safe return to play.
A baseline cognitive assessment should be completed as part of the preparticipation physical examination.
The traditional approach to a diagnosis of concussion relying on loss of consciousness has great limitations and underestimates concussions. C

Be sure to evaluate the neck carefully for cervical spine trauma, and obtain radiographs if any discomfort is present or if the mechanism of injury suggests cervical spine trauma, such as axial loading injuries. C
The Canadian Head CT rule and New Orleans Criteria are clinical rules for minor head injury and are useful for identifying which patients need neuroimaging. B
For pediatric patients, the PECARN clinical prediction rule has been shown to be sensitive in identifying those that need CT imaging.
Strict grading systems have been abandoned in favor of an individualized approach to assessment and treatment.

This is based on an evaluation of risk factors, such as age, history of prior concussions, duration of symptoms, response to exercise, and an assessment of cognitive functioning, with CT scanning reserved for patients with possible intracranial bleeding.

While loss of consciousness is a commonly discussed feature, it is not required for the diagnosis of concussion. Typical cognitive features, symptoms, and physical signs are listed below. Cognitive features: confusion, amnesia, loss of consciousness, lack of awareness of the period, opposition, or score of the game. Typical symptoms: headache, balance problems or dizziness, nausea, feeling dinged, stunned, or dazed, visual problems, hearing problems, irritability. Physical signs: loss of consciousness, poor coordination/balance, convulsion, slow to answer, poor concentration, inappropriate emotions, vomiting, vacant stare, slurred speech, personality changes, significantly decreased playing ability.

Be sure to evaluate the neck carefully for cervical spine trauma, and obtain radiographs if any discomfort is present or if the mechanism of injury suggests cervical spine trauma, such as axial loading injuries.
Neuropsychological testing is useful for assessing the severity of concussion.

Neuroimaging is not routinely recommended for simple concussive injury. CT is recommended if you suspect that an intracerebral structural lesion exists, as shown by prolonged disturbance of conscious state, focal neurologic symptoms, or worsening symptoms.

In children with acute mild traumatic brain injury (TBI), commonly called concussion, the best evidence from a review of guidelines suggests considering head CT only for children with severe headache, worsening symptoms, or in whom a head or neck injury is also suspected. Skull x-rays do not have a role in mTBI management, and routine imaging is also not supported by high-quality evidence.
The Canadian Head CT rule and the New Orleans Criteria are clinical rules for minor head injury are also useful for identifying which patients need neuroimaging.

A systematic review concluded that among adults with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 13 or higher after traumatic brain injury (TBI), severe intracranial injury is present in approximately 7%. The absence of ALL features on the Canadian CT Head Rule lowered the probability of severe head injury to 0.31%, while the absence of all features on the New Orleans Criteria lowered it to 0.61%.

Clinically significant CT findings aremore likely in patients with head trauma and decreasing level of consciousness, loss of consciousness of more than 5 minutes, palpable depressed skull fracture, signs of basilar skull fracture, or abnormal Glasgow Coma Score.
Finding a clinically significant brain hemorrhage on imaging is rare six hours after injury with no clinical deterioration (0.03%)

Based on the PECARN prediction rules, CT is recommended for pediatric athletes with one of the following: GCS <15, a palpable skull fracture (if < 2 years of age), signs of a basilar skull fracture (if > 2 years of age), or altered mental status.

In a prospective observational study of the need for head CT scans among 20,137 children with head injuries, three clinical prediction rules PECARN, CATCH, and CHALICE were 89-100% sensitive in ruling out serious injury.
Assessment tools have been developed and validated to guide identification of concussion.
Neurocognitive testing increases diagnostic accuracy when used in conjunction with self-reported symptoms.
The Sport Concussion Assessment Tool-5th edition (SCAT5) is used for sideline evaluation in athletes >13 years of age and the Child SCAT5 is used for athletes ages 5-12 years of age.

The Standardized Assessment of Concussion (SAC), which is part of the SCAT, assesses four domains (orientation, immediate memory, concentration and delayed recall) for use on the sideline at athletic events and is 80% to 94% sensitive and 76% to 91% specific for identifying concussion.
The Balance Error Scoring system (BESS) assesses postural stability in 5 minutes and is less accurate than the above tests (sensitivity 34%, specificity 87%).
Recent studies have shown support for vestibular/ocular-motor screening (VOMS) to identify those with sports-related concussions

The Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) and Graded Symptom Checklist (GSC) are symptom checklists that are easily administered, and have sensitivities ranging from 64% to 89% and specificities ranging from 91% to 100%.

Clinical prediction rules have been developed and validated to predict the risk of more severe intracranial injury requiring intervention using the PECARN rule in children age 2 to 18 and the need for CT imaging in children using the CATCH2 rule.
Another clinical rule predicts the likelihood of post-concussion syndrome in children with head injury.
See for the approach to an athlete with suspected head injury.

An athlete should be removed from play if there is any suspicion for a concussion, including loss of consciousness, seizure, amnesia, tonic posturing, motor abnormalities, or symptom recurrence with exertion.
Concussions impair one's sensorimotor functioning, doubling the chances of an athlete sustaining a musculoskeletal injury with continued play.
Continued play after a concussion versus immediate removal also significantly increases an athlete's chance of a protracted recovery by nearly nine times.

Clinical prediction rules have been developed and validated to predict the risk of more severe intracranial injury requiring intervention using the PECARN rule in children age 2 to 18 and the need for CT imaging in children using the CATCH2 rule.
Another clinical rule predicts the likelihood of post-concussion syndrome in children with head injury.

Guidelines from the American Academy of Neurology concluded that data was insufficient to conclude that any intervention either hastens recovery or decreases long-term consequences after a concussion. C

No player should be allowed to return to play until concussive symptoms have resolved and off medications given specifically to treat concussive symptoms. However, there is no evidence to support bedrest.B

Referral to a concussion specialist is recommended in adult athletes with continued symptoms at 10-14 days, in pediatric patients with continued symptoms at 1 month,, and those with a history of multiple concussions, depression, and mood disorders.
Return to play protocol should follow a medically supervised, stepwise process () based on symptoms. However, prescribed bed rest is not necessary.C
Clinical trial evidence to support the use of pharmacological therapy in the treatment of concussion is largely lacking.
A small crossover randomized trial in patients with traumatic brain injury (range mild to severe, with loss of consciousness) found that melatonin improved sleep quality and duration.
Over-the-counter analgesics, such as acetaminophen and ibuprofen, may be used for symptomatic relief of headache.

A systematic review of anticonvulsants to prevent seizure in adults with mild to moderate traumatic brain injury found 8 studies with 5637 patients. The most widely used anticonvulsants were levetiracetam, phenytoin, and valproic acid. In the studies, the rate of post-traumatic seizures ranged from 0% to 4%. The overallabsolute risk reduction (ARR) was only 0.6%, with a number needed to treat of 167. For patients with mild injuries, the ARR was also 0.6% (95% CI 0.01% - 1.2%). This small benefit must be balanced against potential harms.

A systematic review identified 41 randomized trials with 4434 patients evaluating medical therapy to improve cognition after traumatic brain injury. Only methylphenidate was found to have any effect on cognitive function, and that was limited to patients with TBI (14 studies of 385 patients). The effect was small (Cohen’s d = .34; 95% CI .12 - .56) and heterogeneity among the studies was moderate.
Athletes should have physical and cognitive rest for 24-48 hours after a concussion, followed by resuming sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise.
Strict rest has been proven to have no benefit, leading to more daily post-concussive symptoms and slower symptom resolution.

A meta-analysis of 7 studies with a total of 269 participants found that symptoms resolution was slightly better in children who returned to normal activity rather prescribed rest (standardized mean difference = 0.39; 95% CI 0.15 - 0.63). Quality of life is not affected by rest versus return to normal activity, and the rate of return to pre-injury activity levels could not be assessed. The authors concluded that children who have experienced a concussion should not be placed on bed rest but instead may return to their previous activity level as allowed by the development of new and worsening symptoms.

A randomized clinical trial in 13-18 year old athletes showed that sub-symptom aerobic exercise within the first week post-concussion decreased recovery time compared to placebo-like stretching group.
A recent systematic review showed that sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise improved symptoms in those with post-concussive syndrome.
In addition to standard physical therapy, vestibular therapy can benefit those with persistent vestibular-ocular symptoms, as these can lead to impaired clinical recovery.
Convergence insufficiency has been found to be present in greater than 40% of those with sports-related concussion.
A randomized trial of 125 persons with GCS 15 and minor head injury found that avoiding video screens for 48 hours increased the proportion who recover.
Emotional symptoms typically develop later in the course of a concussion.

Individuals with a history of mental health issues, notable life stressors, and baseline traits of irritability, anxiety, and depression are at a greater risk for suffering from post-concussive syndrome, however those with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or other learning disabilities are not at significantly increased risk.

Sports psychology may have a potential application, particularly in those with persistent post-concussive syndrome. A systematic review concluded that cognitive behavioral therapy may be effective for treatment of postconcussion symptoms.
Social support has been proved to have a significant effect on adherence to rehabilitation.
Varies greatly from athlete to athlete.
A concussion with minimal symptoms can usually be treated with rest and continued observation alone
No player should be allowed to return to play until concussive symptoms have resolved.
The return to play protocol should follow a medically supervised, stepwise process ().

Recommendations for hospitalization include deteriorating level of consciousness, skull fracture, penetrating skull injury, focal neurologic signs, loss of consciousness greater than 5 minutes, persistent vomiting or headache after injury, lack of responsible supervision, multiple concussions in the same event.

Also hospitalize any patient with clinically significant abnormalities on imaging, those who have not returned to a GCS score of 15, or those in whom drug or alcohol intoxication precludes assessment.
If the patient is hospitalized, monitor him/her at least every 30 minutes while the score is less than 15.
Neurosurgical consultation is unlikely to change the management of a patient with mild TBI and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15.
Clinically significant and potentially disabling symptoms persisting beyond 28 days is referred to as persistent postconcussive symptoms (PPCS).

Predictors for PPCS include the following: (a) a prior concussion with symptoms lasting longer than one week; (b) physician-diagnosed migraine history; (c) sensitivity to noise; (d) fatigue; (e) answering questions slowly; (f) abnormal tandem stance; (g) age 13 years or older; (h) female sex; and (i) headache. For low-risk patients (0-3 of these features) the negative likelihood ratio is 0.36, and for high-risk patients the positive likelihood ratio was 3.0.
Dizziness, post-traumatic amnesia, and abnormal Romberg testing are on-field symptoms that have recently been described in literature to be associated with risk of PPCS
Fatigue and tandem stance errors were also found in clinic patients to independently be associated with PPCS.
The syndrome is less common in countries where litigation following accidents is uncommon.
Reassurance and education about the effects of concussion have been shown to reduce the incidence and duration of post-concussive symptoms at 6 months.

Other treatments of PPCS include antidepressants for poor concentration or sleep; meclizine or vestibular exercises for dizziness; and mild analgesics. However, these have not been studied in controlled trials.
A controversial and deadly complication is the second impact syndrome, which is thought to be secondary to diffuse cerebral swelling, with delayed catastrophic deterioration.

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is currently being investigated as a potential long term deleterious effect of repetitive head trauma and progressive neurodegeneration. Symptoms can range from behavioral and mood disturbances to cognitive impairment.
Players with previous concussion are nearly six times more likely to have future concussive injury. B
Athletes with three or more prior concussions are more likely to sustain more severe concussions with longer recovery times. B
Female gender is associated with significantly higher risk of poor outcome following TBI. B
Long-term sequelae may include low self-esteem, loneliness, antisocial behavior, and prolonged memory deficits.
Chronic pain, primarily headache, is common in persons who have had a mild TBI.
A study of 1282 children initially evaluated for acute head trauma in a US ED found no long-term impact on intelligence as measured by IQ.
Women are at risk for worse outcomes than men.
Players with previous concussion are nearly six times more likely to have future concussive injury.
Athletes with three or more prior concussions are more likely to sustain more severe concussions with longer recovery times.

In a prospective study of 341 adults in New Zealand, 50% of adults and older teens with mild TBI (defined as loss of consciousness for <30 minutes and disorientation for <24 hours) experienced 4 or more post concussive symptoms 1 year later (i.e. headaches, dizziness, nausea/vomiting, noise sensitivity, fatigue, irritability); and 10% experienced some cognitive dysfunction.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of former athletes (retirement >10 years prior) showed that those with a history of concussions had decreased cognitive performance later in life (deficits in verbal memory, recall and attention).

A study in professional soccer players found that they were more likely to have a neurodegenerative disease on their death certificate (especially Alzheimer disease) than matched controls (2.9% vs 1.0%, NNTH = 52). They were also more likely to have been prescribed a medication for dementia.
The return to play after a concussion should proceed in a stepwise fashion ().
If any postconcussion symptoms occur during above progression, the athlete should drop back to the previous level and try to progress again after 24 hours.
Neurocognitive testing is an important component in any return to play protocol.
Patients should be instructed to return to the hospital if they experience increasing headache, weakness, gait difficulty, vomiting, or fluid leaking from nose or ear (basilar skull fracture).

In children aged 8 to 12, who play youth football, the incidence of concussion is 1.76 per 1000 athletic exposures, the majority of which were from head-to-head contact and were 25 times more common in games than in practice.
Among children (average age 15.2) with prolonged symptom duration from a sports-related concussion, the only predictor of prolonged recovery was the total score on the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale.

A 2019 study showed that symptom improvement occurred mainly in the first two weeks for children and the first four weeks for preadolescents and male adolescents, with female adolescents having a protracted recovery.
Because of the different physiologic response during childhood head trauma, a conservative return to play approach is recommended.

A large prospective cohort was used to develop a clinical decision rule. It demonstrated that a head CT scan was not indicated if the child had a GCS of 15, no altered mental status, and did not have at least one of the following:
For children <2 years old: abnormal behavior, loss of consciousness for >5 seconds, a scalp hematoma (excluding frontal), a palpable skull fracture, or a severe mechanism of injury. For children >2 years old: vomiting, any loss of consciousness, severe headache, or a severe mechanism of injury.

algorithm.title: Sideline Algorithm for Suspected Head Injury in Athletes

feature.caption: Canadian CT Head Rule for Minor Head Injury.
feature.feature_body:
Among adults with blunt head trauma within the previous 24 hours resulting in loss of consciousness, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation and a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 15, CT is required if they meet one or more of the following criteria: High risk for neurologic intervention: GCS score <15 at 2 hours after injury Suspected open or depressed skull fracture Any sign of basal skull fracture (hemotypmanum, “raccoon” eyes, cerebrospinal fluid otorrhea or rhinorrhea, or Battle’s sign) Two or more episodes of vomiting Age of 65 years or more
Medium risk for brain injury on CT: Amnesia before impact greater than 30 minutes Dangerous mechanism (pedestrian struck by motor vehicle, occupant ejected from motor vehicle, fall from height greater than 3 feet or five stairs)

feature.caption: New Orleans Criteria for Minor Head Injury.
feature.feature_body: Among adults with blunt head trauma within the previous 24 hours resulting in loss of consciousness, definite amnesia, or witnessed disorientation and a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 15, CT is required if they meet one or more of the following criteria: Headache Vomiting Older than 60 years Drug or alcohol intoxication Persistent anterograde amnesia (deficits in short-term memory) Visible trauma above the clavicle

feature.caption: Recommended Sequence for Return to Play Following a Concussion.
feature.feature_body: 24-48 hour physical and cognitive rest. Symptom limited activity. Light aerobic exercise, no resistance training. Sport-specific exercise. Noncontact training drills. Full contact training after medical clearance. Game play. If any postconcussion symptoms occur during the above progression, the athlete should drop back to the previous level and try to progress again after 24 hours. From McCrory, et al.
